questions.prompt: An LTI system is driven by \(\cos(\omega t)\). In sinusoidal steady state, its output is…
options: a sinusoid at frequency \(2\omega\) with the same amplitude
a sinusoid at the same frequency with exactly the same amplitude and phase
a sinusoid at the same frequency \(\omega\), with a different amplitude and phase
questions.explanation:
Sinusoids/complex exponentials are eigenfunctions of LTI systems: the output is the input scaled by a complex number \(H(j\omega)\), which changes only the amplitude (by |H|) and the phase (by \(\angle H\)).
LTI systems never change the frequency, and they only leave amplitude and phase untouched if \(H=1\).

questions.prompt: What is \(d/dt\) of the complex exponential \(e^{j\omega t}\)?
questions.explanation:
\(d/dt\ e^{j\omega t}=j\omega\ e^{j\omega t}\). That is why derivatives become multiplications by \(j\omega\) and integrals become divisions by \(j\omega\).
• \(e^{j\omega t}/(j\omega)\) is the INTEGRAL.
• Dropping the j loses the 90° rotation.
• \(-j\omega\ e^{-j\omega t}\) is the derivative of \(e^{-j\omega t}\), not \(e^{j\omega t}\).

questions.prompt: An LTI system has \(H(j\omega)=\dfrac{3}{2+j\omega}\). The input is \(x(t)=4\cos(2t)\) (t in seconds). What is the amplitude of the steady-state output?
questions.explanation:
At \(\omega=2\): \(|H|=3/|2+j2|=3/\sqrt{8}=1.061\). The output amplitude is \(4\times1.061=4.24\).
• Using \(H(0)=1.5\) gives 6: that is the DC gain, not the gain at \(\omega=2\).
• \(3/(2+2)\) adds the real and imaginary parts instead of taking \(\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\), giving 3.

questions.prompt: A linear system obeys \(2\cdot dy/dt+3y=x(t)\), with \(x(t)=6\cos(1.5t)\ (t\) in seconds). What is the steady-state amplitude of y?
questions.explanation:
Let \(x=X\ e^{j\omega t}\) and \(y=Y\ e^{j\omega t}\). Then \(d/dt\to j\omega\): \(2j\omega Y+3Y=X\) ⇒ \(H(j\omega)=Y/X=1/(3+j2\omega)\).
At \(\omega=1.5\): \(H=1/(3+j3)\), \(|H|=1/\sqrt{9+9}=1/(3\sqrt{2})=0.2357\).
Amplitude \(=6\times 0.2357=1.414\) (phase −45°).
Common mistake: forgetting the 2 in \(2j\omega\) (using \(3+j\omega=3+j1.5\) gives amplitude 1.79).

questions.prompt: A first-order low-pass has \(H(j\omega)=1/(1+j\omega\tau)\) with \(\tau=2\ \mathrm{ms}\). For a 250 Hz sinusoid, what is the phase of the output relative to the input, in degrees? (Give a negative number for a lag.)
questions.explanation:
\(\omega=2\pi\cdot 250=1570.8\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\), so \(\omega\tau=1570.8\times 0.002=3.142\).
\(\angle H=-\tan^{-1}(\omega\tau)=-\tan^{-1}(3.142)=-72.34^{\circ}\).
Common mistake: using f instead of \(\omega\ (\omega\tau=0.5\) gives −26.6°), forgetting the \(2\pi\).

questions.prompt: A system obeys \(d^{2}y/dt^{2}+3\cdot dy/dt+2y=x(t)\). Using complex exponentials, which expression is \(H(j\omega)=Y/X\)?
questions.explanation:
Substitute \(x=Xe^{j\omega t}\), \(y=Ye^{j\omega t}\): \(d/dt\to j\omega\) and \(d^{2}/dt^{2}\to(j\omega)^{2}=-\omega^{2}\). Then \((-\omega^{2}+j3\omega+2)Y=X\), so \(H=1/((2-\omega^{2})+j3\omega)\).
• \((j\omega)^{2}=-\omega^{2}\), not \(+\omega^{2}\) (first wrong choice).
• The first-derivative term keeps its j (second wrong choice dropped it).
• The second derivative gives \(-\omega^{2}\), which is REAL; it is not \(-j\omega^{2}\) (third wrong choice).

questions.prompt: A system obeys \(\ddot y+4\dot y+3y=6x\). For the input \(x=\cos(t)\), by how many degrees does the steady-state output lag or lead the input? (Negative for a lag.)
questions.explanation:
Replace \(d/dt\) by \(j\omega\): \(H(j\omega)=\dfrac{6}{3-\omega^2+j4\omega}\). At \(\omega=1\): \(H=\dfrac{6}{2+j4}\), so \(\angle H=-\tan^{-1}(4/2)=-63.4^\circ\), a lag.
• \(-\tan^{-1}(4/3)=-53.1^\circ\) forgets the \(-\omega^2\) from the second derivative.
• A positive angle comes from putting the denominator's angle in the numerator.
• \(-90^\circ\) is only reached at \(\omega=\sqrt3\), where the real part vanishes.
questions.figure_alt: Input cosine (solid) and a smaller output cosine (dashed) that lags it.

questions.prompt: A high-pass system has \(H(j\omega)=j\omega\tau/(1+j\omega\tau)\). It is driven by \(x(t)=5+2\cos(\omega t)\), where \(\omega\tau=1\). Which steady-state output is correct?
questions.explanation:
Superposition: the DC term \((\omega=0)\) and the AC term are treated separately, each multiplied by H at its own frequency.
• DC: \(H(0)=0\), so the offset of 5 is completely blocked.
• AC at \(\omega\tau=1\): \(H=j/(1+j)=(1/\sqrt{2})\angle 45^{\circ}\), so the output is \(2\times 0.7071\ \cos(\omega t+45^{\circ})=1.414\cos(\omega t+45^{\circ})\).
Mistakes: scaling the DC by \(|H(j\omega)|=0.707\) (giving 3.54) or passing it unchanged (5); a high-pass leads, not lags (phase +45°, not −45°).
questions.figure_alt: Input waveform: a 2 cosine riding on a 5 DC level.

questions.prompt: A system described by a real-coefficient differential equation has \(H(j\omega_0)=0.5\angle-40^\circ\). What is its steady-state response to \(x(t)=\sin(\omega_0t)\)?
questions.explanation:
A sine is just a cosine shifted by \(-90^\circ\), and the same scaling and phase shift apply to it: the output is the input with amplitude times \(|H|\) and \(\angle H\) added to its phase. Real coefficients guarantee \(H(-j\omega)=\overline{H(j\omega)}\), which is why the real-part trick works for sines too.
• Switching to cosine changes the waveform by 90°.
• \(+40^\circ\) flips the sign of the phase shift.
• The extra minus sign would be an additional 180° shift that H does not contain.

questions.prompt: Preview of transfer functions. A system obeys \(\dot y+5y=2\dot x+x\). What is \(|H(j\omega)|\) at \(\omega=5\ \mathrm{rad/s}\)?
questions.explanation:
Both sides get \(j\omega\): \((j\omega+5)Y=(2j\omega+1)X\), so \(H=\dfrac{1+j2\omega}{5+j\omega}\). At \(\omega=5\): \(|1+j10|/|5+j5|=10.05/7.07=1.42\). The ratio of polynomials in \(j\omega\) is exactly what the transfer-function skill writes as \(H(s)\).
• Ignoring the \(\dot x\) term gives \(1/7.07=0.141\).
• Using \(H(0)=0.2\) gives the DC gain.
questions.figure_alt: Bode magnitude of (1 + 2 j omega)/(5 + j omega): low at DC, rising between the zero and pole, flat at high frequency.

questions.prompt: Preview of the frequency-domain view. A system's sinusoidal gain is measured as 0.9 at 1 rad/s, 0.45 at 10 rad/s and 0.05 at 100 rad/s. What kind of system is it?
options: A band-pass system with a peak at 10 rad/s
A low-pass system: it passes slow inputs and attenuates fast ones
Not LTI, since the gain changes with frequency
questions.explanation:
The gain falls as frequency rises, which is the definition of low-pass behavior. Near 100 rad/s the gain drops roughly tenfold per decade, the signature of one dominant pole. Gain that depends on frequency is perfectly normal for LTI systems; only creating new frequencies would rule LTI out.
• A high-pass would grow with frequency.
• A band-pass would rise and then fall; here 10 rad/s is not a maximum.
questions.figure_alt: Measured gain points falling with frequency, joined by a dashed low-pass curve.

questions.prompt: Preview of Bode plots. A cascade of two buffered low-pass stages has \(H(j\omega)=1/[(1+j\omega/\omega_{1})(1+j\omega/\omega_{2})]\) with \(\omega_{1}=10^{3}\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\) and \(\omega_{2}=10^{5}\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\). For the input \(2\cos(\omega t)\) at \(\omega=10^{4}\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\), what is the steady-state output amplitude? (Magnitudes of a product multiply.)
questions.explanation:
\(|1+j\omega/\omega_{1}|=|1+j10|=\sqrt{101}=10.05\); \(|1+j\omega/\omega_{2}|=|1+j0.1|=\sqrt{1.01}=1.005\).
\(|H|=1/(10.05\times 1.005)=0.09901\). Amplitude \(=2\times 0.09901=0.198\).
Notice the first pole does almost all the work; the second pole (still ten times away) only trims about 0.5%. This is the kind of reasoning that makes Bode plots fast.
